newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Menem calls U.S. sanctions "unjust".
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Menem calls U.S. sanctions "unjust".

text.p: President Carlos Menem Thursday condemned U.S. sanctions against what it regards as insufficient Argentine patent protection for drug firms, but hinted at a possible compromise.

"It is a totally unjust sanction which has no bearing on reality, but it does not damage in the least the excellent relations between the United States and the Republic of Argentina," Menem told local television.
He added "Anyway, we will continue talking to see how we can overcome this situation."
Menem's comments came after his brother Eduardo, a senior senator, said earlier Thursday that Argentina will not toughen up its laws to please the United States.
"We are not going to pay any attention to any of this," Senator Menem told local radio. He added, "Parliament has already fixed its position and we are going to keep it."

While government officials insist no laws will be changed to appease U.S. wrath, the government has yet to decree the regulation of a confidentiality law annex to intellectual property legislation, which could give it room to maneuver.
But the head of the lower house of Congress' Industry Committee rejected appeasement Thursday, calling instead for retaliation against the United States, according to the state-run Telam news agency.

"If we give in to the pressures from the United States, which originate with American drug firms, we would have to boost the price of drugs by up to 70 percent," said Humberto Roggero, a member of the governing Peronist Party.
Washington said Wednesday it would withdraw half of Argentina's duty-free trade benefits as Argentine laws failed to protect intellectual property rights of U.S. drug labs.
U.S. Trade Representative-designate Charlene Barshefsky said the action would affect about $260 million worth of Argentine exports to the United States.
Argentine media estimated the move would cost $10-20 million in lost exports, and officials said they did not think Washington would be able to impose tougher sanctions.

"Our laws comply with GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade), and so that reduces their scope for sanctions. If they did we would be able to officially complain," said Jorge Campbell, Economic Relations Secretary earlier in the week, when Argentina received a letter from President Bill Clinton advising of the U.S. sanctions.
Campbell said the U.S. move was a tough political gesture but of little economic significance.
Barshefsky said the new Argentine patent laws passed in 1995 and 1996 still allow Argentina's pharmaceutical companies to freely copy drugs developed by U.S. firms.
The United States has been pressing Argentina for years to reform its laws on intellectual property rights, which until 1995 set no restrictions on copying foreign drug patents.

Menem, who has sought to strengthen Argentina's diplomatic ties with Washington, proposed legislation that would have pleased the United States, but his bills were either blocked or watered down by the Argentine Congress.
